title: Memory-pressure and graceful-degradation guidelines for runtime
content:
Goal

Short: define pragmatic guidelines and a lightweight state machine for how the serving runtime should respond to memory pressure and OOMs so customer workloads degrade gracefully rather than hard-failing. This doc focuses on interactions between kernel selection, request scheduler, KV cache, and retry/circuit-breaker policies.

Context / motivation

We see two broad failure modes at scale: transient memory spikes (large prompt + large batch + long context) and persistent pressure due to slow KV cache evictions or memory leaks. Currently a small number of customer incidents surface as sudden 503s or full process OOMs. We need consistent behavior across hosted/dedicated/private: predictable fallback flow, clear telemetry, and a set of defensive tactics that are cheap to implement and low-risk to correctness.

Non-goals
- This is not a full scheduler redesign.
- Not prescribing exact kernel code; focus is on coordination and policy.

Assumptions
- Runtime exposes: per-request memory estimate, model sequence length, kv-cache residency size, and current free memory at the process/gpu level (from host agent).
- Kernels have coarse memory profiles: small, medium, large. We can switch to a lower-memory kernel variant if available (e.g., faster quantized kernel vs full fp16) with known quality/perf tradeoffs.
- Scheduler supports preemption of queued requests and controlled rejection.

High-level strategy (3 tiers)
1) Soft mitigation (no user-visible failure): delay, shed batching, shrink micro-batch, use fallback kernel, drop non-essential request features (e.g., tool-calling)
2) Intermediate mitigation (graceful degradation): accept request but reduce max_output_tokens, enforce truncated prompt, force quantized model variant, use local KV-cache miss policies (disable prefetch)
3) Hard mitigation (protect process): fast-fail (503) with clear retryable flag OR routing to lower-capacity lane / different instance pool; trigger circuit-breaker and alerting

Decision surface (policy inputs)
- free_memory_pct (host + gpu free percent)
- estimated_request_mem (based on seq length, batch_size, model variant)
- kv_cache_pressure_pct (kv size / kv_capacity)
- recent_oom_count (windowed per-process)
- queue_length and batch_wait_time
- kernel_variant_availability (list)
- customer-tier (hosted vs dedicated vs private)

Suggested runtime state machine (simplified)
- NORMAL: accept requests -> attempt to allocate kernel path -> OK
- CONGESTED: triggered when free_memory_pct < M1 (e.g., 25%) or kv_cache_pressure_pct > K1 (e.g., 80%) -> enter soft mitigation for new requests for a short window (10s)
- STRAINED: if pressure persists for T1 (e.g., 30s) or recent_oom_count > N1 -> enter intermediate mitigation for longer window (2m) and escalate telemetry
- PROTECT: if severe (free_memory_pct < M2 e.g., 10%) or process OOM observed -> hard mitigation, stop accepting new requests, mark instance unhealthy, trigger rollout/fallback routing, and increment circuit-breaker counter

Notes on action mapping to components
- Scheduler: apply lower batch sizes, disable packing across requests, prefer single-request micro-batches; optionally increase scheduling delay (hold for additional 5-10ms) to form safer batches. Also surface per-request note if it was delayed due to pressure.
- Kernel selector: prefer lower-memory kernel variants when switching is expected to reduce working set (e.g., switch to 4-bit quant variant or attention kernel with streaming KV). Kernel variant selection must be idempotent and safe for cached KV states.
- KV cache: actively shrink per-tenant or tenant-group caches. Eviction policy: prefer LRU across request prefixes but with a bias to keep recent prefixes for long-running chat sessions. Implement 'graceful eviction' where we persist a short hash of evicted KV so that subsequent requests can detect cache miss and fetch full KV incrementally.
- Retry / client-facing behavior: soft mitigations should not return 5xx. If intermediate mitigation reduces quality (e.g., quantized variant or truncated context), return response with header/metadata flags: x-redwood-degraded: true and x-redwood-degradation-reason: memory_pressure_quantized or context_truncated. Hard mitigations return 503 with retry-after and a machine-readable error_code (OOM_PROTECT) so SDKs can implement exponential backoff + jitter.

Circuit breaker semantics
- Per-instance circuit-breaker that trips when PROTECT entered more than C1 times in rolling window W1 (e.g., 3 times in 10 minutes).
- When tripped, instance is marked NEEDS_RESTART and taken out of normal routing; requests routed to fallback pool. The breaker resets after auto-recovery window or manual restart.
- We should expose per-customer and per-route breakers too (to isolate noisy tenants). Breaker counters: oom_count, hard_reject_count, degraded_response_count.

KV-cache specific recommendations
- Two-tier cache: hot-kv (in-memory, fast eviction threshold) and cold-kv (local disk or pinned host memory as fallback). On pressure, move some cold entries to disk-backed store rather than keeping everything resident.
- Adaptive per-tenant caps: use recent qps/latency to allocate KV quota; when pressure, reduce quota multiplicatively for low-priority tenants.
- Prefetch backoff: reduce async prefetch concurrency when free_memory_pct < prefetch_thresh.
- Optional compactification: periodically recompute compressed KV blobs (e.g., delta-encoded key-values) during low load windows to reduce working set.

Retry and backoff guideline for clients
- For responses with 5xx/503+OOM_PROTECT: client SDK should retry automatically with exponential backoff up to R1 attempts (default 3) unless error contains non-retryable flag.
- If server returns x-redwood-degraded: true, SDK should surface a warning but not retry. Provide a telemetry hook so customers can opt-in to monitor degraded outputs.

Telemetry and observability
- Emit events for state transitions: congestion_start, congestion_escalate, protection_entered, protection_exit. Include metrics: free_memory_pct, kv_pressure_pct, kernel_variant, recent_oom_count.
- Track per-request annotations: degradation_applied (list), delay_ms, kernel_variant_used, kv_hit_ratio_pre/post.
- Provide a dashboard: per-pool memory pressure heatmap, top tenants by kv_consumption, instances with repeated breaker trips.

Quick recovery playbook (runbook items)
1) Auto actions: when PROTECT triggers -> drain instance, clear caches, restart serving process (if auto-restart enabled), mark instance out of rotation.
2) If restart fails or repeated trips: escalate to SRE with automatic snapshots of heap/gpu-alloc state and last 1k requests.
3) Customer communication: if a dedicated customer is impacted, send incident note with: degrade flags observed, time window, suggested client-side retries.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- How aggressive should kernel switching be? Frequent switching can thrash caches and lead to regressions. We should enforce a cooldown (e.g., 30s) between kernel changes per-instance.
- Can we safely quantize mid-request for long-running streaming sessions? Likely not without recomputation. Prefer switching per-new-request only.
- Disk-backed cold-kv helps but adds latency tail risk; need SLA tradeoffs for dedicated customers.
- For multi-tenant instances: what's the fairness policy for eviction? Do we prefer per-tenant quotas or global LRU with priority tags?

Implementation tasks (MVP)
- [ ] Add free_memory_pct and kv_cache_pressure metrics to host agent and expose via runtime telemetry API. (owner: Marcus)
- [ ] Implement basic state machine in scheduler with NORMAL/CONGESTED/STRAINED/PROTECT and policy knobs. (owner: Aisha)
- [ ] Kernel selector changes: accept low-memory fallback variants and cooldown logic. (owner: Elena)
- [ ] KV cache: implement eviction bias and prefetch backoff. (owner: Diego)
- [ ] SDK: surface degraded response headers and update default retry logic. (owner: devexp)

Appendix: example flow (timeline)
- t0: normal. Incoming large prompt (40k tokens) + batch_size=4 -> estimated_request_mem exceeds per-request estimate.
- t0+5ms: scheduler marks request as CONGESTED and applies soft mitigation: reduce micro-batch to 1 and select quantized kernel (if available). Response starts streaming with x-redwood-degraded: true.
- t0+30s: multiple such requests push free_memory_pct under 10% -> transition to PROTECT. New requests get 503 OOM_PROTECT and instance added to breaker counter. Telemetry emits protection_entered.
- Auto-restart triggered, KV cache evicted of low-priority tenants, instance restarts and recovers to NORMAL.

Next steps
- Review with SRE and Product to finalize thresholds M1/M2/K1/T1.
- Add a small user study for degraded outputs quality when using quantized kernels so we can baseline acceptable loss.
- Prototype the state machine as a feature flag on a small pool and measure false positives and customer impact.

Notes-to-self
- Keep this doc deliberately implementation-agnostic; follow up with concrete PRD for kernel-contract changes and SDK header spec.
- Add references to existing oom-mitigation playbook after merging.

Unresolved links / TODOs
- Need mapping table: kernel_variant -> expected_mem_reduction and perf impact (ms per token)
- Decide default cooldown and condenser windows
